items.title: English in a Minute: Pie in the Sky
texts: Welcome to English in a Minute.
Pie is a delicious dessert!
And there are so many different flavors, like cherry, lemon, banana cream!
But what could the idiom “pie in the sky” mean?
Pedro is finally moving to Hollywood to follow his acting dream.
He’s been talking about that for years.
His plans are just pie in the sky.
His YouTube channel has over four million subscribers!
Four million? Hmm.
Anything “pie in the sky” could be great but probably won’t happen.
As an adjective, “pie in the sky” describes dreams, goals, or plans that are unlikely to become reality.

items.title: English in a Minute: On the Ball
texts: Welcome to English in a Minute!
Some people use a large ball for exercise.
Is that what to get “on the ball” means?
Hi Anna! How has your day been?
Great! Very great! Very productive!
I finished three reports and have only one more to do!
Wow, you are on the ball!
How did you do them so fast?
Coffee! Lots of coffee. Do you want some?
I’ll get it. I’d love more coffee. Thank you!
Uh, sure. But maybe not that much coffee.
Someone who is “on the ball” finishes work quickly and ahead of time.
We can also say a person should “get on the ball” when they need to work faster or better.
And that’s English in a Minute!

items.title: News Words: Illusion
texts: Welcome to the Voice of America’s News Words.
A museum in Miami, Florida specializes in works of art that stretch the imagination.
Illusion.
The Miami Paradox Museum is one of several paradox museums across the world.
More than 70 of its displays produce optical illusions worthy of a photograph.
The museum explains the math and science behind each illusion.
An illusion is anything that is false or not real but that seems to be true or real.
An optical illusion tricks your eyes to make you think you see something that is not present or that looks different in reality.

items.title: Everyday Grammar Video: Goodbye In Informal Conversations
texts: In an earlier lesson we talked about ways to say goodbye.
We only had time for the formal ways, like “Goodbye” and “Have a good day.”
Today, we want to teach some informal ways to part from a friend.
If you think you will see them soon, you might say, “See you soon” or “See ya’ soon.”
When we speak informally, we often use the reduced vowel, or schwa, which sounds like “uh.”
In writing, you might see this written with “ya” as in “See ya later” or “See ya’ around!”
The structure for these expressions is verb, with an optional preposition, plus “you” plus time.
For example: See you later.
One example with a preposition is, “Talk to you later.”
So we might say, “see you tomorrow” or “catch you next week.”
Sometimes we just use “until” with “later” or another time word.
For example, “Until tomorrow.”
I’ve heard people just say, “later.”
And sometimes we are saying goodbye to someone we don’t expect to see again soon.
In that case, we wish them well.
At the goodbye party for Mary, I heard some of those.
One was “Take care of yourself and stay in touch.”
Right. If someone is leaving on a trip, you can wish them a safe journey, with “Have a safe trip!”
Or we can say, “Drive safely.”
Well. I have to go now, John.
As our friend Anna says, “Until next time!”
Later, Jill! And that’s Everyday Grammar!
